To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) ICT can be a powerful tool for people with disabilities to participate and be heard in the e-governments of their communities; (2) the e-governors of local governments are not yet ready to provide this access; (3) people with disabilities are ready to participate in local government, and (4) people with disabilities can be empowered to demand that their local governments provide them with this access.

ICT offer a promising technology that citizens with disabilities can use to participate in local governance, but that the e-goverance landscape is heterogeneous, reflecting differences among the disability community as well as the online governance entities, and that systematic changes to the development and implementation of local e-goverance for people with disablilities are needed.

1) people with disabilities face a variety of barriers to participation in e-governance; 2) the e-governments are not designed to meet the needs of people with disabilities and 3) the e-goverments are not designed for people with disabilities to participate effectively in e-governments.

there is no single, simple solution to the problem of e-governance and people with disabilities, but rather a series of solutions, some of which may be more appropriate than others, depending on context.

the ICT landscape for people with physical disabilities in the context of e-governance is heterogeneous, and the development, implementation and evaluation of e-governed services must account for this heterogeneity.
